opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underrated analogies out there. The farm animal welfare example is interesting because, if you'd asked people fifteen years ago whether you could get the biggest food companies in the world to commit to going cage-free, a lot of people would have said that's naive. You'd think you need legislation, or you need consumers to change their behavior. What advocates found was that you could go directly to companies with a fairly specific, achievable ask, and through a combination of persuasion, reputational pressure, and the sense that "your competitors are doing it," get a huge number of them to commit. Then a lot of those commitments actually got implemented, though not all of them, and follow-up has been a big part of the work.

So when I think about AI, the question is: what's the equivalent of the cage-free pledge? I think it's something like getting AI companies to adopt concrete safety practices: evaluating models for dangerous capabilities before deploying them, having pre-committed plans for what they'll do if those evaluations come back concerning, investing in information security so model weights don't get stolen, and having some kind of external accountability for all of it. The responsible scaling policy idea is roughly in this spirit. You're asking a company to say, "Here's what we'll do if we see X," in a way that's checkable.

There are some important differences, though. In animal welfare, the ask is relatively cheap for the company. Cage-free eggs cost a bit more, but it doesn't threaten the core business. With AI, some of the most important safety measures could mean slowing down or not deploying something in a very competitive race, and that's a much bigger ask. Also, with cage-free, everyone basically knows what a cage-free egg is. With AI safety, the science of what counts as "safe enough" is immature, so there's a real risk of commitments that sound good but are vague enough that they don't bind anyone when it matters.

So I'd say a few lessons carry over. One, be specific; vague asks don't produce much. Two, start with the companies most likely to say yes and use them to create a norm, because once a few leaders adopt something, the laggards look bad. Three, don't treat the commitment as the finish line. A lot of the real work in animal welfare has been tracking whether companies follow through, and I think that will be even more true for AI, where you need some form of credible auditing or transparency.

And I'd add that I don't see this as a substitute for regulation. In animal welfare, corporate commitments and legislation have reinforced each other. Voluntary practices at the leading AI companies can become the template for what eventually gets codified. If you can show a practice is workable because several companies are already doing it, that makes it a lot easier for policymakers to require it across the board. So I think of corporate advocacy as a way to make progress now, while the policy conversation is still catching up, and to build the foundation for something more durable later.

r001.rationale: The response compares the cost and difficulty of safety commitments with cage-free pledges, but does not suggest AI companies are more resistant to protests.

r002.rationale: It notes that AI safety is scientifically immature and that vague commitments may not bind companies, but does not say developing practical demands makes up more of the advocacy work than in farm animal welfare.

r003.rationale: The response calls for follow-up, auditing, and transparency, but does not identify iterative work inside a company as a way to develop less costly safety measures.

r004.rationale: It mentions competition between companies as a source of reputational pressure, but not competition for safety-conscious talent or willingness to adopt inexpensive measures with little external pressure.

r005.rationale: The response mentions reputational pressure, but does not propose using media attention to safety practices to give responsible companies a recruiting advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underappreciated analogies, and it's one I've thought about a fair amount because Open Philanthropy was involved in both areas.

So the basic story in farm animal welfare is that for a long time, a lot of the energy went into things like trying to get people to go vegetarian, or trying to pass legislation, and both of those are really hard. What ended up being, I think, one of the most cost-effective things anyone did in that space was this corporate campaign model: you pick a specific, concrete ask — cage-free eggs is the canonical example — and you go to companies one at a time. You say, "Here's a commitment we'd like you to make. Here's a reasonable timeline. If you make it, we'll say nice things about you. If you don't, we're going to run a campaign pointing out that you're lagging behind your competitors." And a lot of the leverage came from the fact that once a few major companies committed, it became kind of embarrassing not to, and it became a de facto industry standard that then eventually got easier to write into law.

I think there's a pretty direct translation to AI, and in some ways the translation is more promising than people realize, because the AI industry has this feature that there's a small number of frontier developers. In farm animal welfare you're dealing with hundreds of restaurant chains and grocery chains. In AI, there are maybe a handful of companies that really matter for the frontier right now. So in principle the "one company at a time" approach is actually more tractable.

The way I'd think about it is: what's the analogue of cage-free? You want asks that are specific, verifiable, and that a company can actually commit to without it being an existential threat to their business. So things like: publish a frontier safety policy — what some people call responsible scaling policies — that says here are the capability thresholds that would cause us to pause or add protections, and here's how we'd evaluate for them. Commit to external evaluations before deployment. Commit to certain security standards for model weights. Commit to a certain level of transparency about incidents. Those are the kinds of things where you can look at a company and say, "Have they done this or not?" in a reasonably binary way.

And then the second piece is the competitive dynamic. One thing that was really powerful in the animal space was the scorecards — just ranking companies publicly on these dimensions. I think that's very underused in AI. If you had a credible third party saying, "Here are the five or six frontier labs, here's how each of them does on these ten concrete practices," I think that creates a lot of pressure, because these companies really do care about their reputation with employees, with policymakers, with customers. And it's a lot easier for people inside a company who want to do the right thing to win an internal argument if they can point to a public comparison.

Now, I want to flag the ways the analogy breaks down, because I think they're important. One is that in farm animal welfare, the thing you're asking for is pretty well understood. We know what a cage is. With AI safety, there's a lot more genuine uncertainty about what the right practices even are. So you don't want to lock in a bad standard just because it's measurable. That argues for asks that are more about process and transparency than about specific technical mandates — "tell us what your plan is and show us you're following it" rather than "do exactly this thing."

The second difference is that the stakes of a company defecting are different. If one grocery chain doesn't go cage-free, that's bad, but it's bounded. In AI, the worry is that a single actor racing ahead could matter a lot. So I think the corporate advocacy approach is best thought of as a complement to, not a substitute for, government action. Part of what it does is it builds the norms and the track record that make regulation more feasible, because regulators can say, "Look, the leading companies already do this voluntarily, we're just making it universal." That's exactly how it went with cage-free in several states.

And the third thing is just that there's a real risk of the advocacy becoming adversarial in a way that's counterproductive. In the animal space, the adversarial dynamic was sort of fine — the companies were never going to be your friends. In AI, a lot of the people who are most worried about safety work at these companies, and you want to keep those relationships functional. So I'd want the version of this that's more like, "We're going to hold you to a high standard and praise you publicly when you meet it," with the campaign stick being more of a background threat than the default move.

But overall, yeah — I think if you asked me, "What's a model from another cause area that AI safety people should be studying more closely?", this would be near the top of my list. It's a proven playbook for getting a concentrated set of actors to adopt costly standards they wouldn't have adopted on their own, and that's exactly the problem we have.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic analogy is that you look for a concrete change that a relatively small number of companies could make, and then try to build pressure and support for that change. In animal welfare, you can ask a company to adopt a particular sourcing policy. You don’t have to persuade everyone to agree with your whole worldview to get something useful done.

For AI, you could imagine asking companies to commit to evaluating their systems for dangerous capabilities before releasing them, to getting independent scrutiny, or to having a plan for what they’ll do if those evaluations turn up something concerning. The ask would be: agree in advance that there are circumstances where you would slow down or stop, and specify how you’ll determine whether you’re in those circumstances.

But I think a lot of the difficulty is in figuring out what to ask for. You want a commitment that actually reduces risk, that you can tell whether a company is honoring, and that doesn’t just become a public relations exercise. With AI, the technology is changing quickly, and we have substantial uncertainty about which measures will help.

So I’d be interested in borrowing the discipline of corporate advocacy: identify the decision-makers, develop a specific ask, make compliance observable, and follow up. But I wouldn’t assume that the same campaign tactics will transfer directly. There’s a lot of technical and policy work needed to make the ask a good one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is interesting. In farm animal welfare, you can identify a relatively small number of companies, ask them to make specific changes, and potentially affect a huge number of animals. With AI, there may also be a relatively small number of companies whose decisions matter enormously. So getting those companies to adopt better practices could be a very high-leverage approach.

The hard part is figuring out what to ask for. With animal welfare, you can have a fairly concrete demand, like moving away from cages. With AI safety, “make your systems safe” isn’t a very useful demand by itself. You need something specific enough that a company can implement it and outsiders can tell whether it’s happening, but that also meaningfully reduces risk.

One possibility is asking companies to commit in advance to evaluating their systems for dangerous capabilities, and to having stronger safeguards—or pausing further development or deployment—if those evaluations reveal sufficiently serious risks. Then there’s a role for outside organizations in assessing those commitments, tracking whether companies follow through, and pushing for improvements.

I’d be cautious about assuming the tactics transfer directly. But the general idea—develop concrete asks, build the expertise to judge whether they matter, and create incentives for a few very important actors to adopt them—seems quite promising to me.
